body:
God keeps His word in the dark.

These notes follow the teaching movement by movement, with the study woven into each section and the passages gathered in full. The question running through them is simple: how do you trust His hands when you cannot see His work?

Open · God has not left you

How do you know God hasn’t left you?

You prayed. You waited. What you prayed about is still unresolved. After a while, the question changes. You still want to know when things will change, but now you are wondering whether He is with you at all.

That is where this message begins. With the person who still believes God and is finding it hard to hope again.

Still waiting after the victory

Genesis 15 follows Abram’s rescue of Lot and his refusal of the king of Sodom’s reward. He has come through a battle. He has refused wealth. But the promised child has not come.

One part of his life has moved forward. The ache remains.

It is possible to have something to thank God for and something you still need to bring Him. Abram’s victory has not answered the question waiting for him at home.

Genesis 15:1-8
1 After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Do not fear, Abram, I am a shield to you; Your reward shall be very great.” 2 Abram said, “O Lord GOD, what will You give me, since I am childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?” 3 And Abram said, “Since You have given no offspring to me, one born in my house is my heir.” 4 Then behold, the word of the LORD came to him, saying, “This man will not be your heir; but one who will come forth from your own body, he shall be your heir.” 5 And He took him outside and said, “Now look toward the heavens, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” And He said to him, “So shall your descendants be.” 6 Then he believed in the LORD; and He reckoned it to him as righteousness. 7 And He said to him, “I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to possess it.” 8 He said, “O Lord GOD, how may I know that I will possess it?”Genesis 15:1-8 · NASB1995

Look back at what Abram has just refused.

Genesis 14:22-23
22 Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have sworn to the LORD God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, 23 that I will not take a thread or a sandal thong or anything that is yours, for fear you would say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’Genesis 14:22-23 · NASB1995

He does not want the king of Sodom to be able to claim responsibility for making him rich. His refusal gives weight to the words about protection and reward at the beginning of Genesis 15. God speaks to a man who has faced kings and declined wealth. The setting helps us hear the reassurance, even though Genesis does not give us a list of the fears in Abram’s mind.

The victory and the refusal are real acts of faithfulness. Neither has removed the ache about a child. We can honor what God has already done without asking the unresolved part of our lives to become silent.

Tell Him what still hurts

God speaks before Abram does. His first words address Abram’s fear. He names Himself as Abram’s shield and promises a reward ahead.

Abram answers by naming what is missing. He is childless. Eliezer remains the heir of his house. He brings the unresolved thing directly into the conversation.

Waiting can make that difficult. You have asked so often that asking again begins to hurt. You stop mentioning it. People may assume you have made peace with it because you no longer say anything.

Proverbs 13:12
12 Hope deferred makes the heart sick, But desire fulfilled is a tree of life.Proverbs 13:12 · NASB1995

The proverb gives words to what waiting can do to a heart. Abram gives us a picture of someone telling God about it. You can tell Him exactly what is still unresolved.

The stars, and still no child

God takes Abram outside. The promise becomes something he can look up at: descendants beyond his ability to count.

But Abram does not return from that encounter carrying a child. He has God’s word about a future he cannot yet see. Verse 6 tells us that he believes the Lord, and the Lord reckons it to him as righteousness.

Keep that order in view as the chapter unfolds. Abram believes before the deep sleep, before the great darkness, before the fire passes between the pieces.

His faith is already real while he is still waiting.

The next chapter gives us a later point in that waiting, when Sarai gives Hagar to Abram.

Genesis 16:3
3 After Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, Abram’s wife Sarai took Hagar the Egyptian, her maid, and gave her to her husband Abram as his wife.Genesis 16:3 · NASB1995

The ten-year marker belongs to that later scene. Genesis 15 does not give us that same date. What it does give us is the order of this encounter: God speaks, Abram believes, and the promised child has yet to arrive. His faith is being exercised before he can point to the fulfillment. We need that order when we are tempted to recognize faith only after a story has a visible resolution.

Bring God the question

After the promise of descendants comes the promise of land. Abram asks how he may know he will possess it. The man who has just believed God is still asking Him for assurance.

The questions concern different promises: descendants in verses 4–5, land in verse 8. Verse 6 tells us that Abram believes God. We do not need to turn Abram into someone who has stopped believing in order to hear the need in his question. He wants assurance about what God has said.

Abram was promised a child. I cannot promise you one. His story does not give me permission to attach God’s name to every outcome we long for. But you can bring God that ache. You can ask for relief. You can tell Him that you are afraid to hope again.

You don’t have to carry that question alone. Bring God the question, even if it is the only prayer you have left.

God’s answer to Abram begins with strange instructions: bring the animals.

Movement One · Covenant assurance

Abram asks how he may know he will possess the land. God tells him what to bring. The answer begins taking shape on the ground in front of him.

A path between the pieces

Genesis 15:9-11
9 So He said to him, “Bring Me a three year old heifer, and a three year old female goat, and a three year old ram, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon.” 10 Then he brought all these to Him and cut them in two, and laid each half opposite the other; but he did not cut the birds. 11 The birds of prey came down upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.Genesis 15:9-11 · NASB1995

A heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon. Abram divides the three animals and lays the halves opposite each other. He leaves the birds whole. Between the pieces is a path.

The scene is difficult to look at. We should let it be. A covenant is being made, and the divided animals give the commitment a visible seriousness. The Hebrew expression often rendered literally as cutting a covenant is an idiom for making one. Here, the account also gives us animals that have actually been cut.

“A covenant like this one was not signed. It was walked.”

Abram has laid out the pieces. He drives away the birds of prey as the day continues. He has done what God told him to do, and he is still waiting for the answer to unfold.

There is something familiar in that distance between doing what you know to do and understanding what comes next. Obedience can be quite definite while the future remains unclear. Abram knows which animals to bring. He does not yet know everything God is about to tell him.

A broken word, and people harmed

Jeremiah gives us another account of people passing between the pieces of an animal. In Jerusalem, the people covenant to release their Hebrew servants. The people release them, then take them back into slavery.

Jeremiah 34:8-22
8 The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people who were in Jerusalem to proclaim release to them: 9 that each man should set free his male servant and each man his female servant, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman; so that no one should keep them, a Jew his brother, in bondage. 10 And all the officials and all the people obeyed who had entered into the covenant that each man should set free his male servant and each man his female servant, so that no one should keep them any longer in bondage; they obeyed, and set them free. 11 But afterward they turned around and took back the male servants and the female servants whom they had set free, and brought them into subjection for male servants and for female servants. 12 Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying, 13 “Thus says the LORD God of Israel, ‘I made a covenant with your forefathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, saying, 14 “At the end of seven years each of you shall set free his Hebrew brother who has been sold to you and has served you six years, you shall send him out free from you; but your forefathers did not obey Me or incline their ear to Me. 15 Although recently you had turned and done what is right in My sight, each man proclaiming release to his neighbor, and you had made a covenant before Me in the house which is called by My name. 16 Yet you turned and profaned My name, and each man took back his male servant and each man his female servant whom you had set free according to their desire, and you brought them into subjection to be your male servants and female servants.”’ 17 “Therefore thus says the LORD, ‘You have not obeyed Me in proclaiming release each man to his brother and each man to his neighbor. Behold, I am proclaiming a release to you,’ declares the LORD, ‘to the sword, to the pestilence and to the famine; and I will make you a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth. 18 I will give the men who have transgressed My covenant, who have not fulfilled the words of the covenant which they made before Me, when they cut the calf in two and passed between its parts— 19 the officials of Judah and the officials of Jerusalem, the court officers and the priests and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf— 20 I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their life. And their dead bodies will be food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth. 21 Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their life, and into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has gone away from you. 22 Behold, I am going to command,’ declares the LORD, ‘and I will bring them back to this city; and they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire; and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant.’”Jeremiah 34:8-22 · NASB1995

Read the reversal slowly. People who had been given their freedom are brought back into bondage. The broken word has entered their homes and their bodies. They are the ones living with what the powerful decided they no longer wanted to honor.

God recalls Israel’s own deliverance from slavery as He confronts them. Their treatment of their neighbors contradicts the mercy in their own history. They have also made their commitment before Him, in the place bearing His name. What they do to these people matters to the God whose name they invoked.

That is why judgment belongs in this passage. It tells us that the suffering of those taken back is being seen and answered. We cannot make covenant-breaking sound small by speaking only about the intentions of the people who broke their word.

The divided calf and the judgment announced against those who passed between its pieces also help us understand the seriousness of such a ceremony. Reading the act as an oath that invokes judgment upon the covenant-breaker fits Jeremiah’s account. Genesis does not spell out every part of that meaning for Abram’s ceremony. We can take the connection seriously while keeping that distinction clear.

This reaches into the promises we make. A promise can shape what another person risks, plans, or entrusts to us. When we break it, the damage may reach further than the moment in which we changed our minds. God’s faithfulness should make us more attentive to the people depending on our word.

Why a covenant answers the question

Abram asks how he can know he will possess the land. The ceremony does not put him in possession of it that evening. God gives him assurance while fulfillment remains future.

Notice where that assurance begins. Before Abram asks his question, God identifies Himself as the One who brought him out of Ur and speaks of the land He will give him. The promise comes from the God who has already acted in his life. Now the covenant will solemnly affirm His commitment to what He has said.

Abram will still have to live toward a future he cannot inspect. God gives him reason to trust the One speaking to him about it. That is a different kind of certainty from having every step explained. He can know who has committed Himself before he knows how the years will unfold.

This matters when we ask God for assurance. We often want enough information to remove the need to wait. God shows Abram that he can depend on His word while he waits. The assurance rests on the speaker’s faithfulness.

We need to remain precise about the promise. God has spoken to Abram about descendants and land. We cannot take the strength of God’s commitment to him and attach it to an outcome God has never promised us. We can learn to trust His character and bring our desires to Him honestly. We can also ask what He has actually given us His word about.

The animals are laid out. The question is before God. Now the chapter takes us into the dark, where the covenant will be made.

Movement Two · Grace in the dark

Faith before the darkness

Genesis 15:12
12 Now when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and behold, terror and great darkness fell upon him.Genesis 15:12 · NASB1995

Abram has already believed God. Now terror and great darkness fall upon him. Those things belong to the same chapter, and they happen to the same man.

Keep the order. Faith is named in verse 6. The deep sleep comes in verse 12. God gives covenant assurance to a man who already trusts Him.

God speaks to Abram while he lies in that deep sleep. He tells him what his descendants will face and what lies ahead in his own life. Later, the smoking oven and flaming torch pass between the pieces. The Lord makes His covenant with Abram. The assurance he asked for comes through what God says and does.

We can begin to treat pain as evidence against our faith. We prayed. We trusted Him. What hurt still hurts. Then another question follows: if God were with us, wouldn’t something have changed by now?

Abram’s story gives us reason to slow down before reaching that conclusion. The darkness did not erase what verse 6 said about his faith. The chapter never asks us to choose between his believing and his fear. It lets us see God meeting him there.

That gives a trembling person room to pray. You do not have to report a confidence you cannot feel. Tell God what frightens you, and bring His word into that same conversation. You can tell Him you are afraid and still trust what He has said.

Generations inside the promise

Genesis 15:13-16
13 God said to Abram, “Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not theirs, where they will be enslaved and oppressed four hundred years. 14 But I will also judge the nation whom they will serve, and afterward they will come out with many possessions. 15 As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace; you will be buried at a good old age. 16 Then in the fourth generation they will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet complete.”Genesis 15:13-16 · NASB1995

God speaks in the darkness. What He tells Abram includes oppression, judgment, and return. His descendants will suffer in a land that is not theirs. God will judge the nation they serve. They will come out, and a later generation will return.

Four hundred years means generations of people whose lives would be spent waiting. The duration is part of God’s answer to a man asking for assurance. We should allow that to trouble the assumption that a reassuring word from God must mean the hardship is nearly over.

Abram is also told about his own death. His life and the full course of his descendants' history will not fit within the same span of years. He can receive a true promise whose fulfillment extends beyond what he will personally live to witness.

Notice, too, that the people who enslave his descendants remain accountable. God announces judgment upon them. The promised return does not make their oppression good or excuse the oppressor. We have to carry the suffering and the judgment with us when we speak about the eventual deliverance.

The Amorites appear in the answer as well. God places the return of Abram’s descendants within His dealings with other peoples. Abram receives a promise concerning his family, but the account gives him a glimpse of a history larger than his household. It leaves much unexplained. It also keeps him from being the only person whose future matters in the scene.

For us, this passage puts care into the way we speak to someone who is waiting. We can pray for relief without announcing that the wait is almost finished. We can acknowledge what they are enduring without treating the eventual good as an explanation for every injury along the way. God has given Abram assurance while telling him plainly that the road will be hard.

The fire passes

Genesis 15:17-21
17 It came about when the sun had set, that it was very dark, and behold, there appeared a smoking oven and a flaming torch which passed between these pieces. 18 On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, “To your descendants I have given this land, From the river of Egypt as far as the great river, the river Euphrates: 19 the Kenite and the Kenizzite and the Kadmonite 20 and the Hittite and the Perizzite and the Rephaim 21 and the Amorite and the Canaanite and the Girgashite and the Jebusite.”Genesis 15:17-21 · NASB1995

The sun has set. Abram is lying still. The smoking oven and flaming torch pass between the pieces, and the Lord makes His covenant with Abram.

The account places the action with God. Abram is not described as passing through. God commits Himself to the promise He has spoken, and the words that follow identify its recipients and its land. The scene reaches a definite covenant declaration rather than ending with an unexplained sign in the night.

God speaks and acts here, in the dark. Abram cannot see how the promise will come to pass, but the Lord is making His commitment. We cannot look at this darkness and say that God has gone.

This is where the title of the message comes into view. Grace in the dark: God giving a frightened person His word. The ceremony answers Abram’s need by directing him toward the faithfulness of the One who makes the promise.

God keeps His word in the dark.

We should let that assurance keep its proper shape. This chapter gives Abram a covenant; it does not give every reader a private map of what God is doing behind the scenes. There will be things we cannot explain. Our hope rests in the God who has made Himself known, even when our knowledge of a particular situation remains incomplete.

So when you cannot see what comes next, you can begin with what God has revealed of Himself. Bring Him the fear. Ask for the help you need. The next step may be small, and the larger question may remain. You are allowed to trust Him without pretending you have been shown the whole road.

With the question still unanswered

Job helps us stay honest about what meeting God may mean for someone who is grieving.

Job 42:1-6
1 Then Job answered the LORD and said, 2 “I know that You can do all things, And that no purpose of Yours can be thwarted. 3 ‘Who is this that hides counsel without knowledge?’ Therefore I have declared that which I did not understand, Things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.” 4 ‘Hear, now, and I will speak; I will ask You, and You instruct me.’ 5 “I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear; But now my eye sees You; 6 Therefore I retract, And I repent in dust and ashes.”Job 42:1-6 · NASB1995

Job encounters God. He does not receive an explanation of why his losses happened. His response includes a changed understanding of his own limits and a deeper knowledge of the One he has been addressing. The encounter is real even though the explanation he might have wanted has not been supplied.

Job was faithful before he lost anything. I will not tell you that you had to lose what you loved to know God. Nor can the later restoration of his fortunes become a schedule for someone else’s recovery. The people he lost cannot be reduced to an amount that was later repaid.

Receiving God’s presence does not require you to call the loss good. You can grieve, ask why, and still turn toward Him. You may carry a question for the rest of your life. The unanswered question does not prevent you from asking Him to meet you in the life you have now.

Psalm 139 speaks directly to the fear of being hidden from God.

Psalm 139:11-12
11 If I say, “Surely the darkness will overwhelm me, And the light around me will be night,” 12 Even the darkness is not dark to You, And the night is as bright as the day. Darkness and light are alike to You.Psalm 139:11-12 · NASB1995

The darkness that limits our sight does not limit His. That gives us a way to pray when our feelings tell us we have disappeared. Being unable to sense His nearness is a real experience to bring Him. It does not mean He has lost sight of us.

Deuteronomy places another distinction beside that comfort.

Deuteronomy 29:29
29 “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our sons forever, that we may observe all the words of this law.Deuteronomy 29:29 · NASB1995

There are things God has not disclosed, and there are things He has given His people to live by. We can acknowledge both. A missing explanation does not remove every known responsibility. You may still know that someone needs the truth, that a child needs care, or that you need help. Obedience can begin within what has been made clear while the larger mystery remains.

Isaiah’s words about God’s higher ways come within an invitation to return to Him and receive pardon.

Isaiah 55:7-9
7 Let the wicked forsake his way And the unrighteous man his thoughts; And let him return to the LORD, And He will have compassion on him, And to our God, For He will abundantly pardon. 8 “For My thoughts are not your thoughts, Nor are your ways My ways,” declares the LORD. 9 “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, So are My ways higher than your ways And My thoughts than your thoughts.Isaiah 55:7-9 · NASB1995

That setting matters. These verses direct the hearer toward a God who has compassion and abundantly pardons. We should hear that invitation when we speak about the limits of our understanding. We can admit that we do not know why a loss occurred and still speak clearly about the mercy of the One to whom we are turning.

You do not need to solve the loss before you can pray. You can tell Him what the absence feels like. You can let another person sit with you in it. And you can keep bringing yourself to the God who sees you.

Movement Three · The living Christ

Genesis has shown God committing Himself to His promise. As we follow that promise through Scripture, we also encounter the failures of the people who receive it. The question becomes more searching: how does God’s faithfulness meet people who have broken their own word?

The promise and the later Law

At Sinai, Israel hears God’s words and pledges obedience. The covenant is solemnly affirmed before the people.

Exodus 24:3-8
3 Then Moses came and recounted to the people all the words of the LORD and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice and said, “All the words which the LORD has spoken we will do!” 4 Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. Then he arose early in the morning, and built an altar at the foot of the mountain with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. 5 He sent young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD. 6 Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and the other half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar. 7 Then he took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people; and they said, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient!” 8 So Moses took the blood and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Behold the blood of the covenant, which the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.”Exodus 24:3-8 · NASB1995

Then comes the golden calf.

Exodus 32:1-6
1 Now when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people assembled about Aaron and said to him, “Come, make us a god who will go before us; as for this Moses, the man who brought us up from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.” 2 Aaron said to them, “Tear off the gold rings which are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me.” 3 Then all the people tore off the gold rings which were in their ears and brought them to Aaron. 4 He took this from their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool and made it into a molten calf; and they said, “This is your god, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.” 5 Now when Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it; and Aaron made a proclamation and said, “Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD.” 6 So the next day they rose early and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.Exodus 32:1-6 · NASB1995

The contrast is painful because their earlier commitment was so clear. The people who promised obedience now take part in idolatry. Their failure cannot be explained away as a misunderstanding of whether God had called them to faithfulness.

In that crisis, Moses appeals to the promise God made to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.

Exodus 32:11-14
11 Then Moses entreated the LORD his God, and said, “O LORD, why does Your anger burn against Your people whom You have brought out from the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand? 12 Why should the Egyptians speak, saying, ‘With evil intent He brought them out to kill them in the mountains and to destroy them from the face of the earth’? Turn from Your burning anger and change Your mind about doing harm to Your people. 13 Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants to whom You swore by Yourself, and said to them, ‘I will multiply your descendants as the stars of the heavens, and all this land of which I have spoken I will give to your descendants, and they shall inherit it forever.’” 14 So the LORD changed His mind about the harm which He said He would do to His people.Exodus 32:11-14 · NASB1995

The stars return to the story. Moses recalls God’s word about descendants too numerous to count and the land He had promised them. He brings that earlier commitment into his plea for the people. Their failure is real, and God’s own word gives Moses a reason to intercede.

Paul later makes the relationship between promise and Law explicit.

Galatians 3:15-17
15 Brethren, I speak in terms of human relations: even though it is only a man’s covenant, yet when it has been ratified, no one sets it aside or adds conditions to it. 16 Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, “And to seeds,” as referring to many, but rather to one, “And to your seed,” that is, Christ. 17 What I am saying is this: the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not invalidate a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to nullify the promise.Galatians 3:15-17 · NASB1995

Keep the order in view. God’s promise to Abraham comes before the Law. The Law does not cancel what God had already promised. Paul names Christ as the promised seed, the One in whom the promise finds its fulfillment.

This helps us keep the covenants distinct while seeing their connection. Genesis 15 concerns God’s promise to Abram. Exodus 24 concerns the covenant at Sinai. Jesus will speak of the new covenant in His blood. We follow God’s faithfulness through these texts by attending to what each actually says and then hearing the connections the New Testament makes.

Abraham’s covenant also carries obligations. Genesis 17 makes that plain.

Genesis 17:9-14
9 God said further to Abraham, “Now as for you, you shall keep My covenant, you and your descendants after you throughout their generations. 10 This is My covenant, which you shall keep, between Me and you and your descendants after you: every male among you shall be circumcised. 11 And you shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be the sign of the covenant between Me and you. 12 And every male among you who is eight days old shall be circumcised throughout your generations, a servant who is born in the house or who is bought with money from any foreigner, who is not of your descendants. 13 A servant who is born in your house or who is bought with your money shall surely be circumcised; thus shall My covenant be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant. 14 But an uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that person shall be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant.”Genesis 17:9-14 · NASB1995

The sign of circumcision and the warning attached to it keep us from describing God’s commitment as permission for indifference. Assurance and a responsible response belong in the same account. God’s faithfulness never makes the promises we have made to other people disposable.

That distinction matters for anyone returning to God after failure. We need a reason to believe mercy is possible. We also need to tell the truth about what we have done. Moses' appeal lets us see a plea for mercy that takes both the people’s sin and God’s promise seriously.

Christ bears the curse

At the table, Jesus names the new covenant in His blood.

Luke 22:20
20 And in the same way He took the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood.Luke 22:20 · NASB1995

He speaks about His own death as a life being given for others. The cup directs the disciples toward what He is about to do. His self-giving is the ground of the new covenant. The forgiveness it promises comes through a death He willingly faces.

John makes His willing action explicit.

John 10:17-18
17 For this reason the Father loves Me, because I lay down My life so that I may take it again. 18 No one has taken it away from Me, but I lay it down on My own initiative. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This commandment I received from My Father.”John 10:17-18 · NASB1995

Jesus gives Himself willingly. His death reveals His obedience and love; it does not make the violence of those who crucify Him innocent.

Paul tells us what Christ accomplishes through that death and how it connects with Abraham’s blessing.

Galatians 3:13-14
13 Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us—for it is written, “CURSED IS EVERYONE WHO HANGS ON A TREE”— 14 in order that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we would receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.Galatians 3:13-14 · NASB1995

Follow the movement of the two verses. Christ bears the curse of the Law. In Him, Abraham’s blessing reaches the Gentiles. The promised Spirit is received through faith. The cost of redemption and the life God gives through it belong to the same account.

That is why Abraham’s story belongs in a study about coming to Jesus. Paul brings the promise into his explanation of Christ’s work. The blessing reaches people beyond Abraham’s own nation, and the gift of the Spirit becomes part of the answer to what grace gives us now.

Keep verse 14 beside verse 13 as we continue. The One who forgives gives His Spirit. After we have faced the sin we need to leave behind, we will still need help to live differently. Paul has already brought that help into the promise.

Faith in the risen Christ

Matthew 27:45-50
45 Now from the sixth hour darkness fell upon all the land until the ninth hour. 46 About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, “ELI, ELI, LAMA SABACHTHANI?” that is, “MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?” 47 And some of those who were standing there, when they heard it, began saying, “This man is calling for Elijah.” 48 Immediately one of them ran, and taking a sponge, he filled it with sour wine and put it on a reed, and gave Him a drink. 49 But the rest of them said, “Let us see whether Elijah will come to save Him.” 50 And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice, and yielded up His spirit.Matthew 27:45-50 · NASB1995

At noon, darkness covers the land. Jesus cries out to God, and Matthew leaves the anguish of that cry before us. We should hear it before moving on. His willing self-giving has not made His suffering unreal.

The darkness at the cross recalls Abram’s night and gives us a picture to hold beside it. Paul has already shown us what connects Abraham’s blessing with Christ’s death. Now Matthew lets us hear the anguish of the One who gives Himself for us.

Jesus enters death. And God raises Him.

Acts 2:24
24 But God raised Him up again, putting an end to the agony of death, since it was impossible for Him to be held in its power.Acts 2:24 · NASB1995

The resurrection changes the invitation before us. We are coming to a living person. We can speak now to the One who gave His life. Asking Him for forgiveness, entrusting our grief to Him, and seeking His help are acts of faith in the risen Christ.

Romans brings us back to Abraham and the circumstances in which he believed.

Romans 4:18-22
18 In hope against hope he believed, so that he might become a father of many nations according to that which had been spoken, “SO SHALL YOUR DESCENDANTS BE.” 19 Without becoming weak in faith he contemplated his own body, now as good as dead since he was about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah’s womb; 20 yet, with respect to the promise of God, he did not waver in unbelief but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God, 21 and being fully assured that what God had promised, He was able also to perform. 22 Therefore IT WAS ALSO CREDITED TO HIM AS RIGHTEOUSNESS.Romans 4:18-22 · NASB1995

Abraham’s confidence concerns what God has actually promised. Paul places that confidence beside the reality of Abraham’s aged body and Sarah’s inability to bear a child. Paul acknowledges the physical difficulty and grounds Abraham’s assurance in God’s ability to keep His word.

That gives us a more honest account of faith than pretending the circumstances are easy. Abraham has reason to trust because God has spoken. The faith Paul describes looks to God’s power to fulfill His own promise.

Then Paul tells us why this account matters to us.

Romans 4:23-25
23 Now not for his sake only was it written that it was credited to him, 24 but for our sake also, to whom it will be credited, as those who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, 25 He who was delivered over because of our transgressions, and was raised because of our justification.Romans 4:23-25 · NASB1995

The reckoning of righteousness in Abraham’s story was written for our sake too: for those who believe in the God who raised Jesus from the dead. Paul connects our faith to Christ’s death for our transgressions and His resurrection for our justification. We are brought into a right standing before God through faith, with Christ’s work at the center of that assurance.

This gives the person who feels unworthy somewhere definite to turn. You are not being asked to manufacture a clean history or a convincing feeling. Put your trust in the God who raised Jesus. Bring Him the truth about your life. His work gives you reason to come before you feel strong enough to explain yourself well.

The One you are coming to is alive.

Receive pardon. Face the harm.

Being afraid while you are trying to trust God is not the same as turning your back on Him. Paul holds warning and faithfulness together.

2 Timothy 2:11-13
11 It is a trustworthy statement: For if we died with Him, we will also live with Him; 12 If we endure, we will also reign with Him; If we deny Him, He also will deny us; 13 If we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.2 Timothy 2:11-13 · NASB1995

Read the whole saying. It speaks about life with Christ, endurance, denial, and His faithfulness to Himself. It warns that Christ will disown those who disown Him, and that warning remains when we reach the words about His faithfulness. We cannot use the last line to make the warning disappear.

Neither should we turn a frightened person’s distress into a verdict that they have rejected Christ. Fear alone cannot settle that question. The invitation can be much more concrete: turn toward Him and come. Jesus speaks directly to the person coming to Him.

John 6:37
37 All that the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will certainly not cast out.John 6:37 · NASB1995

There is welcome here for the person returning. You can ask for mercy with an unsteady voice. You can begin telling the truth about what you have done before you have worked out every consequence of confessing it.

David’s confession gives us a brief, sobering picture of pardon.

2 Samuel 12:13
13 Then David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” And Nathan said to David, “The LORD also has taken away your sin; you shall not die.2 Samuel 12:13 · NASB1995

The mercy spoken to him does not make the people harmed by his sin disappear from the story. Pardon and an honest account of the damage can be held together. Psalm 51 lets us hear the need for cleansing and inward renewal at length.

Psalm 51:1-17
1 For the choir director. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Be gracious to me, O God, according to Your lovingkindness; According to the greatness of Your compassion blot out my transgressions. 2 Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity And cleanse me from my sin. 3 For I know my transgressions, And my sin is ever before me. 4 Against You, You only, I have sinned And done what is evil in Your sight, So that You are justified when You speak And blameless when You judge. 5 Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, And in sin my mother conceived me. 6 Behold, You desire truth in the innermost being, And in the hidden part You will make me know wisdom. 7 Purify me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. 8 Make me to hear joy and gladness, Let the bones which You have broken rejoice. 9 Hide Your face from my sins And blot out all my iniquities. 10 Create in me a clean heart, O God, And renew a steadfast spirit within me. 11 Do not cast me away from Your presence And do not take Your Holy Spirit from me. 12 Restore to me the joy of Your salvation And sustain me with a willing spirit. 13 Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, And sinners will be converted to You. 14 Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, the God of my salvation; Then my tongue will joyfully sing of Your righteousness. 15 O Lord, open my lips, That my mouth may declare Your praise. 16 For You do not delight in sacrifice, otherwise I would give it; You are not pleased with burnt offering. 17 The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; A broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.Psalm 51:1-17 · NASB1995

The prayer reaches beyond relief from guilt. It asks for a clean heart, a willing spirit, restored joy, and a life that can again bear witness to God’s mercy. The person confessing needs God to deal with what is within as well as with what has been done.

For us, repentance can take very ordinary forms. Return what you can. Correct the lie you left standing. Stop asking someone else to carry the consequences in silence. Accept accountability, even when it costs you. Those actions do not purchase God’s pardon. They belong to turning from the sin for which you are asking pardon.

The person you hurt does not owe you immediate trust because you have asked God for forgiveness. Some repair takes years. Some consequences remain. Their need for safety and their freedom to tell the truth matter throughout that process.

Your self-punishment cannot add to Christ’s sacrifice. Receive His pardon and face the harm you caused. Grace gives you reason to begin telling the truth and to keep living truthfully when the first emotion of confession has passed.

Movement Four · His Spirit is with you

Forgiveness brings a further question into view. How do we live the life to which God calls us? Galatians has already named the promised Spirit, received through faith. The One who forgives does not leave us to supply the life of obedience from ourselves.

Forgiveness and a renewed heart

Jeremiah describes the new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah.

Jeremiah 31:31-34
31 “Behold, days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, 32 not like the covenant which I made with their fathers in the day I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, My covenant which they broke, although I was a husband to them,” declares the LORD. 33 “But this is the covenant which I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” declares the LORD, “I will put My law within them and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people. 34 They will not teach again, each man his neighbor and each man his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD,’ for they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them,” declares the LORD, “for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more.”Jeremiah 31:31-34 · NASB1995

God’s law will be written within His people. They will know Him, and He will forgive their sins. These promises reach into the relationship itself: what they know of God, what is written on their hearts, and how He deals with their guilt.

That is a fuller account of grace than relief from a charge alone. God addresses the inward life of the people He forgives. The promise brings knowledge of Him and a changed relation to His instruction together with mercy.

Hebrews takes up Jeremiah’s words within its account of Christ’s ministry.

Hebrews 8:6-13
6 But now He has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as He is also the mediator of a better covenant, which has been enacted on better promises. 7 For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion sought for a second. 8 For finding fault with them, He says, “BEHOLD, DAYS ARE COMING, SAYS THE LORD, WHEN I WILL EFFECT A NEW COVENANT WITH THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL AND WITH THE HOUSE OF JUDAH; 9 NOT LIKE THE COVENANT WHICH I MADE WITH THEIR FATHERS ON THE DAY WHEN I TOOK THEM BY THE HAND TO LEAD THEM OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT; FOR THEY DID NOT CONTINUE IN MY COVENANT, AND I DID NOT CARE FOR THEM, SAYS THE LORD. 10 “FOR THIS IS THE COVENANT THAT I WILL MAKE WITH THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL AFTER THOSE DAYS, SAYS THE LORD: I WILL PUT MY LAWS INTO THEIR MINDS, AND I WILL WRITE THEM ON THEIR HEARTS. AND I WILL BE THEIR GOD, AND THEY SHALL BE MY PEOPLE. 11 “AND THEY SHALL NOT TEACH EVERYONE HIS FELLOW CITIZEN, AND EVERYONE HIS BROTHER, SAYING, ‘KNOW THE LORD,’ FOR ALL WILL KNOW ME, FROM THE LEAST TO THE GREATEST OF THEM. 12 “FOR I WILL BE MERCIFUL TO THEIR INIQUITIES, AND I WILL REMEMBER THEIR SINS NO MORE.” 13 When He said, “A new covenant,” He has made the first obsolete. But whatever is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to disappear.Hebrews 8:6-13 · NASB1995

Hebrews names Jesus as the mediator of the better covenant and brings Jeremiah’s promise into its account of His ministry. Israel and Judah remain named in the words it quotes. God confronts His people’s failure to remain in His covenant, and He promises to forgive their sins and write His law within them. Jesus mediates that promised covenant.

Ezekiel also speaks to the restoration of God’s people, naming a new heart and the gift of His Spirit.

Ezekiel 36:26-27
26 Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. 27 I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes, and you will be careful to observe My ordinances.Ezekiel 36:26-27 · NASB1995

Notice how closely the gift of the Spirit and obedience belong together. God promises inward renewal and His own enabling presence. The life He calls His people to live is a life for which they must depend on Him.

That gives us a way to ask for help that reaches beneath appearances. We can ask God to change the resentment we have learned to conceal, the appetite we keep defending, or the desire to be admired for a life we are not actually living. Forgiveness, a new heart, and the Spirit’s help belong together in these promises. We can bring Him the whole need.

Learning to walk with His help

Holiness was never the entrance fee. Holiness is the fruit.

Calling holiness fruit does not make it optional. It tells us to depend on God for the changed life He calls us to live. Paul describes that life concretely.

Galatians 5:16-26
16 But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh. 17 For the flesh sets its desire against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are in opposition to one another, so that you may not do the things that you please. 18 But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law. 19 Now the deeds of the flesh are evident, which are: immorality, impurity, sensuality, 20 idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, disputes, dissensions, factions, 21 envying, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these, of which I forewarn you, just as I have forewarned you, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law. 24 Now those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. 25 If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. 26 Let us not become boastful, challenging one another, envying one another.Galatians 5:16-26 · NASB1995

The conflict in this passage is real. The desires of the flesh and the Spirit are opposed to one another. Paul addresses people who need to keep walking by the Spirit amid that struggle. The presence of temptation does not make his instruction meaningless; it is part of the situation in which the instruction is needed.

Look at how much of the passage concerns our life with other people. Hostility, jealousy, factions, and envy damage a community. The Spirit’s fruit also becomes visible in relationships: in patience when someone is difficult, gentleness when we have power to wound, and self-control when an impulse is demanding to be obeyed.

This gives us something more searching than a general wish to be better. Think about the conversation you keep avoiding, the person whose success makes you resentful, or the reply you want to send while you are angry. Ask for the Spirit’s help there. A changed life takes shape in particular acts of obedience.

Paul warns that a life given over to these practices has no place in God’s kingdom. We are called to turn from what destroys life and to keep walking in the life the Spirit gives. Grace does not invite us to rename a settled practice so that we can keep it undisturbed.

At the same time, obedience can begin before the struggle feels easy. Tell the truth while the lie would still protect you. Ask for help while the temptation is still present. Accept correction while you still feel defensive. You can depend on the Spirit in the very place where you discover how much you need Him.

The Spirit, and still the groaning

Romans 8:23-27
23 And not only this, but also we ourselves, having the first fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our body. 24 For in hope we have been saved, but hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he already sees? 25 But if we hope for what we do not see, with perseverance we wait eagerly for it. 26 In the same way the Spirit also helps our weakness; for we do not know how to pray as we should, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words; 27 and He who searches the hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, because He intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.Romans 8:23-27 · NASB1995

Stay with the order of the passage. Before Paul speaks about help in prayer, he describes people who already have the Spirit and are waiting for the redemption of their bodies. Both things are true at once. God has given them His Spirit, and they still live with suffering and bodily frailty. They have received something real from Him while waiting for what He has promised to complete.

Their groaning belongs inside that waiting. Paul includes himself among them. He can speak with confidence about what God will do and still admit the strain of living before it is finished. That gives us room to name the pain without making our pain the verdict on whether God has been faithful.

Hope reaches toward what is still unseen. That is why waiting belongs in Paul’s account. If everything had already arrived, there would be nothing left to await. The Spirit’s presence and our longing for redemption can occupy the same life.

Then Paul brings us into prayer. The weakness reaches even there: we do not always know what to ask. You may know exactly what is wrong and still be unable to see what would make it right. You may ask for relief and wonder what relief could even look like now.

The Spirit helps in that uncertainty. His intercession is according to God’s will, which means our inability to see the whole situation does not put the whole burden of prayer on our understanding. We bring what we know. God knows what we cannot yet make sense of.

The passage locates our assurance in His help. It does not require a particular sensation to prove that help has begun. You may finish praying with the same ache and without a clear next step. You can return to the promise of His intercession while those things remain unresolved.

Remember who these groaning people are: people who have received the Spirit. You can ask Him for help before you have found the right sentence, and you can keep asking while you wait.

The life in front of you tomorrow

Tomorrow may begin with the same demands. Getting dressed. Answering the phone. Doing what used to come easily. You know what the day requires and do not know where the strength will come from.

Another hard morning does not mean God has left you. Open Romans 8:23–27 again and read the whole movement: the Spirit received, the redemption still awaited, and the help given in weakness. Then tell God what you are facing. You can begin with the words you have: God, I believe You are here, and I am still afraid.

Let the prayer become particular. Name the appointment, the conversation, or the hour you are dreading. Ask for help with what is in front of you. If there is an obedient step you already know to take, take it with His help. If the next step is unclear, you can say that too.

There may also be a person you can call. Someone trustworthy who can hear that the morning is hard without demanding that you explain it away. Tell them what would help: staying on the phone, bringing a meal, going with you, or helping you make the next call. Receiving care belongs in the life you are bringing to God.

Doctors, counselors, and medicine can be part of that care. Treatment is not a failure of faith. Needing it is not evidence of a demon. You can receive prayer and treatment together.

Hold fast to the One who is holding you.

Renewed hope · Bring Him the morning

Ask again, honestly

Trusting God does not require you to stop asking for relief. If asking hurts because you have been disappointed before, tell Him that too.

You can be grateful for what He has given you and still need work. You can thank Him for the people in your life and still be lonely. You can believe He hears you and be afraid to pray the same prayer again. Gratitude and an unmet need can be brought into the same conversation with Him.

Sometimes we try to settle the outcome before we pray. We rehearse why the answer is unlikely, or we decide that needing it this much must mean something is wrong with us. Then the prayer becomes smaller than the need we are actually carrying.

You can name the desire plainly. Ask for healing, provision, companionship, rest. Tell Him where you need relief and what the waiting has done to you. You do not have to make the request impressive or hide the part you are afraid to say.

There is room to ask without claiming you know what His answer must be. Bringing the desire to God lets you be honest about both your need and your dependence on Him. You can ask Him to sustain you as you wait, even while you continue asking Him to change what hurts.

Know what has been promised

The strength of Christian hope depends on the faithfulness of God. It also calls for care in naming what He has promised. Joshua speaks about the Lord’s good promises to Israel coming to pass.

Joshua 21:45
45 Not one of the good promises which the LORD had made to the house of Israel failed; all came to pass.Joshua 21:45 · NASB1995

Joshua is looking back at what God had told Israel He would do. Before we claim this verse over our own situation, we need to ask what God has actually promised.

Paul locates the promises of God in Christ.

2 Corinthians 1:20
20 For as many as are the promises of God, in Him they are yes; therefore also through Him is our Amen to the glory of God through us.2 Corinthians 1:20 · NASB1995

Christ gives us ground for confidence in God. That confidence concerns God’s promises; it does not turn every desire we hold into a promise He has made. We need to be able to distinguish what we are asking for from what God has pledged to give.

The distinction protects the person who is waiting. If I promise you an outcome God has not promised, I may leave you feeling betrayed by Him when my assurance fails. It is more faithful to pray earnestly with you, tell you what Scripture gives us reason to hope for, and remain beside you without pretending to know the future.

Paul gives us another reason to trust God while we wait.

Romans 8:28
28 And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.Romans 8:28 · NASB1995

This promise addresses those who love God and are called according to His purpose. Read it beside the groaning, hope, and Spirit’s intercession that precede it. In the next verse, Paul describes God’s purpose as making His people like His Son. His purpose reaches beyond the relief we are asking for, and His work continues while weakness and waiting are still real.

We do not have to call each painful event good in itself. Nor do we have to identify its benefit before we are allowed to grieve. We can entrust ourselves to God’s purpose while admitting that we cannot yet explain what He will bring from a situation. His faithfulness is not dependent on our ability to produce that explanation.

Hope beyond one lifetime

Hebrews describes people who died in faith without receiving the promises. They had seen them from a distance and welcomed them. Their hope reached beyond the years they lived on earth.

Hebrews 11:13-16
13 All these died in faith, without receiving the promises, but having seen them and having welcomed them from a distance, and having confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. 14 For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a country of their own. 15 And indeed if they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had opportunity to return. 16 But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God; for He has prepared a city for them.Hebrews 11:13-16 · NASB1995
Hebrews 11:39-40
39 And all these, having gained approval through their faith, did not receive what was promised, 40 because God had provided something better for us, so that apart from us they would not be made perfect.Hebrews 11:39-40 · NASB1995

Abraham did receive Isaac. Hebrews does not erase that gift. It looks beyond it, toward the heavenly country and the fulfillment God’s people will share. A particular promise can be fulfilled within a person’s life while the larger hope still reaches ahead.

That keeps us honest when we speak about someone who died while still waiting. Their death does not give us permission to call their faith a failure. Scripture commends people whose lives ended before the fulfillment they awaited. Their hope was directed toward a future that could not be measured by the length of their lives.

This does not make the death easy for those who love them. It gives grief somewhere to turn without demanding that grief disappear. We can miss the person, acknowledge what remains unfinished, and look toward the future God has promised. We do not need to invent an explanation for their death in order to confess that hope.

Psalm 73 gives us language for trusting God when strength itself fails.

Psalm 73:25-26
25 Whom have I in heaven but You? And besides You, I desire nothing on earth. 26 My flesh and my heart may fail, But God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.Psalm 73:25-26 · NASB1995

The psalmist can name the failure of flesh and heart while looking to God as his lasting strength and portion. Trust does not depend on being able to sustain himself. He can depend on God as his own strength fails.

Read that alongside Hebrews, and the horizon of hope becomes larger than the answer we want this week. We can ask for help now and still look toward the fulfillment that belongs to God’s promised future. Both belong in the life of faith.

Receive the good you can receive

You may still be hurting when a friend makes you laugh. Let yourself laugh. You may find rest for an afternoon while the larger question remains. You can receive that rest.

A good moment does not require you to declare the grief finished. Enjoying the meal, accepting the invitation, or noticing something beautiful does not mean you have forgotten what happened. You do not have to save every good thing until everything is fixed.

Neither does a hard day afterward cancel the good you received. You can be thankful for yesterday’s rest and admit that today is difficult. There is no need to force the week into one simple account before you can bring it to God.

Let someone share the good with you when you can. Let them hear the ache when that is what you have. A life can contain both, and there is room for both in prayer.

I am asking God for peace where you have been afraid. For help with what has become too heavy to carry alone. For joy you can recognize and receive, even while you are waiting. You can ask Him to renew your hope without pretending you already know how tomorrow will feel.

The close · Come as you are

Bring the need with you

We began with a question about God’s presence when what we have prayed for remains unresolved. Genesis brought us to a frightened man receiving God’s word in the dark. The New Testament has brought us to Christ, His death and resurrection, and the gift of His Spirit.

Those are the grounds on which we are invited to trust. We can name who He is and what He has done while still admitting what we do not understand about our own lives.

Bring Christ the prayer you are tired of praying. Bring the question you cannot answer. If what you have is anger, tell Him the truth about that too. You can ask Him to change what hurts. You can grieve what you have lost. You may not get the gift you asked for. Receiving the Giver does not require you to call the loss a gift.

Put your faith in the living Christ. Bring the sin you need to turn from. Ask His Spirit to help you trust Him while the way forward is still unclear.

The cup, and the unfinished count

Remember the cup Jesus gave His disciples. He named the new covenant in His blood. The One we are coming to has given His life for us. His promise gives our trust somewhere to rest.

Abraham held Isaac. God gave him the son He had promised.

Genesis 21:5
5 Now Abraham was one hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.Genesis 21:5 · NASB1995

But Abraham died without counting all the descendants God had spoken of beneath that sky. The child in his arms was a real fulfillment, and the promise still reached beyond what he could hold or see.

Paul brings the promise to Christ.

Galatians 3:16
16 Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, “And to seeds,” as referring to many, but rather to one, “And to your seed,” that is, Christ.Galatians 3:16 · NASB1995

The promise leads us to a person, and our invitation can name Him: Jesus Christ, who gave His life for us and rose from the dead.

The bright morning star

Revelation 22:16
16 “I, Jesus, have sent My angel to testify to you these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.”Revelation 22:16 · NASB1995

Jesus names Himself as David’s root and descendant and as the bright morning star. The image gives us hope while it is still dark and turns our attention toward the day He will bring.

We can receive that hope without assigning a date to the answer we want. His promised future gives us reason to look ahead, and His presence gives us reason to ask for help here. Both belong to the hope we confess.

Come with the question still unanswered. You do not have to explain your way out of the dark before you can turn toward God. The One who gave Himself for us and rose again is the One to whom we bring the life we have today.

A prayer to take into tomorrow

Trusting Jesus means coming to Him for forgiveness and entrusting your life to Him as you turn from your sin, even while your feelings are unsettled.

If you are trusting Jesus for the first time, or returning to Him, tell someone who can walk with you. Ask a pastor, elder, or minister to pray with you. You can begin while you are still finding the words.

Jesus, I need You. I don’t know what comes next. I believe You have not left me. Help me trust You here.

Take it into tomorrow morning. You can pray it with the question still unanswered.

God keeps His word in the dark. Come.
